group_assessment.note: Author identity is unambiguous from affiliation and co-author continuity.

corpus_crossquery.query: Which existing LEGEND records depend on PMID 25012504 and do the full panels support their wording?
corpus_crossquery.finding: The core HIF1A axis is supported, but three propagated details required correction: acute blood glucose is not in-vivo glucose uptake; digoxin-associated transcripts are GLUT1/PHD3 rather than PDK1/PHD3; and the reported 100 mg/kg dose remains ambiguous rather than verified as a typo. Corrections are appended as DL-MECH-095.

retraction_check.result: No retraction, expression of concern or correction for PMID 25012504. One background reference in its bibliography is marked retracted and was not used as primary support.

verbatim_locators.source_fulltext_indexed_evidence: Structured PMC HTML and 10-page PDF are local and fingerprinted. Six main figures were inspected at native 731-796 pixel width. The complete legacy PPT was rendered to seven 2000x1500 slide images and inspected; all four pages of the Word legends were rendered and read.
verbatim_locators.abstract_anchoring_waived: All textual locators below are from Results or Discussion, never the abstract; visual locators point to fingerprinted figure artifacts.

entries.proposition: WWOX loss increases glucose uptake cell-autonomously in primary MEFs.
entries.snippet: Remarkably, mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) isolated from KO embryos displayed an increase in glucose uptake as early as 1 h following addition of 2-NBDG
entries.anchor: Results, WWOX deficiency causes a cell-autonomous increase in glucose uptake

entries.proposition: The paper directly measures a glycolytic/respiratory shift rather than inferring it solely from transcription.
entries.snippet: Concomitantly, lack of WWOX causes a reduction in oxygen consumption (Figure 2b), suggesting that in Wwox-deficient cells glucose is utilized primarily for glycolysis, whereas mitochondrial respiration is inhibited
entries.anchor: Results, enhanced glycolysis and reduced mitochondrial respiration

entries.proposition: PDK1, the proposed PDH gate, is directly reported as upregulated in KO cells.
entries.snippet: Notably, we observed higher levels of Pdk1, which phosphorylates and inhibits pyruvate dehydrogenase, the rate-limiting enzyme that regulates entrance of pyruvate into the TCA cycle
entries.anchor: Results, WWOX directly inhibits expression of HIF1alpha target genes

entries.proposition: The first WW domain is required for WWOX rescue of HIF1alpha target-gene expression.
entries.snippet: Importantly, we found that overexpression of intact WWOX, but not a mutant form of WWOX-WFPA, which harbor a mutation in WW1 domain of WWOX that abrogates its interaction ability, in Wwox KO MEFs reduced HIF1α target genes' expression under normoxia
entries.anchor: Results, WWOX directly inhibits expression of HIF1alpha target genes

entries.proposition: WWOX loss raises HIF1alpha protein under normoxia.
entries.snippet: In contrast, HIF1α was readily detected in Wwox KO cells (Figure 3e). HIF1α was also detected in skeletal muscles, which is considered the main peripheral organ involved in glucose uptake, of Wwox KO mice
entries.anchor: Results, WWOX decreases HIF1alpha protein levels

entries.proposition: The WWOX-dependent difference in HIF1alpha abundance disappears under hypoxia in the authors' model.
entries.snippet: Interestingly, we found that WWOX does not affect HIF1α protein levels under hypoxic conditions (Figure 4c), likely as WWOX levels goes down under these conditions
entries.anchor: Results, WWOX is downregulated under hypoxic conditions

entries.proposition: The pharmacological in-vivo result is an acute blood-glucose change, not a flux or neurological endpoint.
entries.snippet: Strikingly, treatment with digoxin caused a fast and specific increase in blood glucose levels specifically in KO mice (Figure 5c)
entries.anchor: Results, knocking down HIF1alpha rescues the metabolic phenotype

entries.proposition: HIF1alpha binding maps to WWOX constructs containing WW1.
entries.snippet: As seen in Supplementary Figure S6A, only GST-WW1 domain-containing vectors were able to precipitate HIF1α
entries.anchor: Results, WWOX physically interacts with HIF1alpha

entries.proposition: Reduced HIF1alpha hydroxylation is observed, while the upstream PHD2 mechanism remains unresolved.
entries.snippet: Using specific antibodies, we found that HIF1α hydroxylation is significantly reduced in WWOX KO MEFs as compared with WWOX WT MEFs (Figure 5f), suggesting that WWOX increases HIF1α hydroxylation leading to its degradation under normoxia
entries.anchor: Results, WWOX physically interacts with HIF1alpha

entries.proposition: The authors explicitly leave PHD2 activity as an open mechanism.
entries.snippet: Whether WWOX affects PHD2 activity is to be determined. Nevertheless, our findings demonstrate that the interaction between WWOX and HIF1α in the nucleus affects HIF1α levels
entries.anchor: Discussion, proposed HIF1alpha degradation route

entries.proposition: Figure 1 visually supports severe systemic hypoglycaemia and increased MEF glucose uptake, but does not itself establish a neural phenotype.
entries.snippet: [figure attestation — pixels cannot be quote-matched] Figure 1: WT blood glucose approximately 130 mg/dl versus KO approximately 10; NBDG uptake KO approximately 2.2-fold versus WT 1, and KO+WWOX approximately 0.25 versus KO+EV 1.
entries.anchor: Figure 1, panels a-d, native 750x470 JPEG

entries.proposition: Figure 2 supports the metabolic shift but shows that succinate is only a non-significant trend.
entries.snippet: [figure attestation — pixels cannot be quote-matched] Figure 2f: fumarate P<0.02, malate P<0.02, succinate P<0.09, fructose-1,6-diphosphate P<0.02. Panel b shows lower KO OCR at baseline and after FCCP.
entries.anchor: Figure 2, panels a-f, native 731x453 JPEG

entries.proposition: Figure 3's rescue uses strongly supraphysiological WWOX transcript expression, which limits dose-equivalent interpretation.
entries.snippet: [figure attestation — pixels cannot be quote-matched] Figure 3b left: KO+WWOX WWOX transcript approximately 25-fold, KO+WFPA approximately 23-fold, KO+EV 1; target-gene rescue is shown in the adjacent graph.
entries.anchor: Figure 3, panels a-f, native 790x605 JPEG

entries.proposition: Figure 4 similarly tests large WWOX overexpression and shows context-dependent target suppression.
entries.snippet: [figure attestation — pixels cannot be quote-matched] Figure 4d-e: WWOX overexpression is approximately 32-fold under normoxia and 28-fold under hypoxia; under normoxia only selected targets fall, while under hypoxia multiple HIF1alpha targets fall.
entries.anchor: Figure 4, panels a-e, native 739x519 JPEG

entries.proposition: Figure 5 bounds the digoxin claim and lacks the promised HIF1alpha-OH densitometry graph.
entries.snippet: [figure attestation — pixels cannot be quote-matched] Figure 5c: KO glucose rises from approximately 10 to 115 mg/dl after 40 minutes of digoxin; WT visually falls from approximately 105 to 75, with no drawn test for that change. Figure 5f contains blots only although the caption announces a graph on the right.

entries.proposition: Figure 6 supports HIF1alpha dependence of transformed KO growth and quantifies a modest human WWOX/GLUT1 association.
entries.snippet: [figure attestation — pixels cannot be quote-matched] Figure 6e table: WWOX+/GLUT1+ 6, WWOX+/GLUT1- 45, WWOX-/GLUT1+ 9, WWOX-/GLUT1- 20, P<0.05. Panels a-c show KO growth suppressed most strongly by shHIF1alpha.
